prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at the magic wavelength enable time and frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my sole prize part, and the round-1 exchange has sharpened rather than changed my reasons. The decisive physical idea is Katori's magic-wavelength condition: choose the trap wavelength so that the light shifts of the two clock levels cancel, and the trap drops out of the measurement. That removes Doppler and recoil effects and allows thousands of neutral atoms to be interrogated at once, which is what turns the clock into a device limited by quantum projection noise and by physics rather than by atom number. Ye's group then took the strontium clock to the 10^-18 regime, with many-body control of the lattice, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and clock comparisons that test the constancy of constants and dark-matter couplings. These are statements about nature, not only about instrument quality. The result has been reproduced and surpassed at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere, which for me is the strongest test of robustness, and the credit chain is short. Every member ranked it in the opening and five of us now name it alone, but I weigh the independent reproduction and the clean two-name chain, not the count.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is that this is an invention and a measurement capability, and a sceptic can say it refines work already recognised in 2005 (the frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems and the ion clocks). The redefinition of the second has not happened, so the largest practical consequence is still ahead. Parallel strontium-clock work by Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams was decisive for accuracy and stability, and a two-name credit cannot honour all of it. I accept these limits and judge that they do not outweigh the combination of a new idea, a new regime and broad independent confirmation.

responses.point: Lindroth finds the novelty of circuit QED hard to separate from cavity QED with atoms (Haroche), sees a second consecutive superconducting-circuit prize as following a theme, and asks how I see the originality relative to atomic cavity QED.
responses.response: The question deserves a direct answer. The regime is the same in kind, but circuit QED is more than a transfer of platform: because the artificial atom has a huge dipole moment and the photon is confined in a one-dimensional resonator, the coupling reaches the strong regime with a margin real atoms never had, and that is what made dispersive readout, on-chip qubit coupling and eventually gate operations possible. I still think that is a distinct achievement. But I concede your other point. A second consecutive superconducting-circuit prize would look like following a theme, and the claim that the originality is separable from Haroche's is at best debatable among colleagues outside my field. Together with my own closeness to the subject, that is why I keep B058 only as an alternative for a later year and do not rely on it. It also strengthens my confidence that the clock stands on a more separable footing.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators (B007), argues that time-reversal-invariant topological insulators are a separate discovery from the 2016 prize, and proposes a citation that credits both the prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation. He admits the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap and the 3D work are outside the trio.
responses.response: I find your 2016 argument largely persuasive: the Z2 classification with time-reversal symmetry and the HgTe edge transport are a separate discovery from Chern-number quantum Hall physics, and I withdraw my earlier worry about conceptual overlap in that sense. My remaining difficulty is the credit chain, not the physics. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction is what told Molenkamp which material and which thickness to grow, so a trio omits the person who closed the loop from theory to experiment, and a citation about the 'first observation' leaves the 3D materials and the ARPES confirmation unsaid, which many will see as the most visible part of the field. If the committee could write a configuration that honours all of this without a visible hole I would support it, but with the three-name limit I do not see it yet. I rank B007 as my first alternative to the clock, above circuit QED.

responses.point: Kroll supports the lattice clock as a source of physics and not merely engineering, judges that waiting for the redefinition of the second is unnecessary, and names Katori and Ye as a defensible credit despite the parallel strontium groups.
responses.response: I agree on all three points, and I would add the criterion I use for the redefinition question: the prize rewards the demonstrated physics, and the performance is already confirmed in several laboratories by direct optical comparisons, so redefinition is a metrological decision that follows the science and not a condition for it. On the credit I would make explicit that the citation should name the invention (magic-wavelength lattice trapping) and the development to the 10^-18 level, so that it neither implies that Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley or the PTB and NIST teams contributed nothing, nor pretends to settle which strontium group came first. I share your reading that Ye's reliance on comb technology is use of an already honoured tool, not a repetition of that prize.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from the Event Horizon Telescope to the optical lattice clock, argues that the clock gives clues from nature (redshift, constants, dark matter) and not only an instrument, but concedes that strictly it is an invention and a measurement capability and that the discovery should be at the centre.
responses.response: I agree that the committee's emphasis on discovery is the right test, and I think the clock passes it more clearly than the word invention suggests. Resolving a gravitational redshift across a millimetre in a many-atom lattice and bounding drifts of constants at this level are results about nature, and the many-body interaction physics seen in the lattice is a new regime of its own. I would ask you to hold the committee to that argument and not to the redefinition of the second, because if the case rests on the redefinition it is a case about metrology. Where I differ slightly is the timing: you see waiting as costless, whereas the independent reproduction is already complete and delay mainly exposes the case to further contested priority claims among the strontium groups.

responses.point: Pearce moved the clock from fifth to first, keeps IceCube as the discovery-led alternative, and asks whether the committee should rely on the atomic physicists for the question of how distinct the lattice clock is from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I think the distinctness question can be answered in terms a non-specialist can check. The 2005 prize rewarded the comb, which counts optical cycles; the 2012 prize rewarded control and measurement of single quantum systems, including the ion clocks. The lattice clock combines a neutral-atom ensemble, a trap engineered so that it does not perturb the transition, and the resulting statistical gain in stability, and none of these is in the earlier citations. I would suggest the committee check the claim by asking whether a reader of the 2005 and 2012 scientific backgrounds could have predicted the magic-wavelength result. I do not think they could, and I would defer to Lindroth and Kroll if they disagree.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a discovery about nature or as precision metrology, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I judge it as the former but this is a matter of reasonable disagreement.

Whether Katori and Ye remain the fairest two-name credit given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and whether any wording can honour the invention without implying exclusion.

Whether a topological-insulator citation can be written for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp without a visible gap for Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang; if it can, B007 is a serious competitor in merit and credit clarity.
How far the redefinition of the second should affect timing, which I judge not to be a condition for recognition.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits and microwave quantum optics, which is the field of the B058 circuit QED candidate (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf). I therefore recuse myself from any decision on B058 and have not relied on it in my preferred configuration; it appears only as an alternative, and I would not oppose the committee discounting it. WACQT leadership is also shared institutionally with Chalmers colleagues on the committee, which Kroll and Mehlig have noted. I have no personal or institutional link to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp, and none that touches B056. If the committee prefers that I abstain from B007 or B056 for any reason, I would accept that.
